incumbent.name: André Carson
incumbent.summary: André Carson has represented the 7th District since 2008 and is seeking a 10th term {wfyi_guide}. In the current Congress he serves on the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee (Aviation; Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials subcommittees), the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, and the Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party {clerk_carson}.
record: May 22, 2025: Voted no on House passage of H.R. 1, the budget reconciliation bill titled the One Big Beautiful Bill Act {roll_2025_145}.
July 3, 2025: Voted no on the motion to concur in the Senate amendment to H.R. 1, the final House vote on the reconciliation bill, which passed {roll_2025_190}.
Nov. 12, 2025: Voted no on H.R. 5371, the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026, the bill that passed the House to end the fall 2025 government shutdown {roll_2025_285}.
Nov. 18, 2025: Voted yes on the Epstein Files Transparency Act (H.R. 4405), which passed under suspension of the rules {roll_2025_289}.

Nov. 19, 2025: Announced his selection as ranking member (top Democrat) of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Subcommittee on Aviation, which oversees civil aviation and the Federal Aviation Administration {carson_aviation_rm}.

Jan. 22, 2026: Voted no on the fiscal year 2026 Department of Homeland Security appropriations bill, saying in a statement that it "continues to fund ICE without any substantive changes to stop unlawful actions and abuse of power" {carson_dhs_vote}.

Feb. 19, 2026: Announced $13.08 million in Community Project Funding for the district, including $1,092,000 for lead service line replacement in Martindale-Brightwood, $1.2 million for IndyGo vehicles and $2 million for an Indianapolis airport baggage-screening system {carson_cpf}.

March 23, 2026: With committee ranking member Rick Larsen, criticized the administration for sending ICE officers to airports during a DHS funding lapse in which TSA agents were working without pay {carson_tsa}.

April 27, 2026: Introduced, with two colleagues, the AI Data Center Site Selection Transparency Act of 2026, which would require communities to be informed of planned AI data centers before deals are finalized {carson_dc_transparency}.

May 15, 2026: His amendment raising VA Medical and Prosthetic Research Program funding to $994 million passed the House as part of the fiscal year 2027 Military Construction-VA appropriations bill, which his office said also includes more than $1.6 billion to replace and modernize the Roudebush VA Medical Center campus in Indianapolis; the bill was sent to the Senate {carson_va_amend}.

May 22, 2026: Voted in the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee to advance the Build America 250 Act surface transportation bill, which included his amendment on motorcycle profiling during traffic stops {carson_build_america}.

June 11, 2026: Introduced the Summer Meals for Kids Act, which would make Summer EBT food benefits a standard part of the National School Lunch Program; his office noted Indiana opted out of Summer EBT {carson_summer_meals}.

June 29, 2026: Joined Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in introducing the AI Data Center Moratorium Act, which would pause new AI data center development until federal safeguards are in place {carson_moratorium}.

Sept. 2, 2026: Sent a congressional inquiry to the Department of Homeland Security seeking data on increased ICE arrests in Indianapolis; his office said he has repeatedly voted against ICE funding and called for eliminating the agency {carson_ice_inquiry}.

Sept. 29, 2026: With Rep. Victoria Spartz (R-Ind.) and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, urged the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to reject BlackRock/Global Infrastructure Partners' application to acquire AES Corporation, AES Indiana's parent, citing utility rates {carson_aes}.

In the 2026 primary, challengers George Hornedo and Destiny Wells criticized Carson; Hornedo cited a Center for Effective Lawmaking ranking of Carson as 197th of 220 House Democrats, and Wells criticized donations from AES Indiana and BlackRock's PAC {mirror_preview}. Carson responded, "I have never, and I will never, allow anyone to impact my vote" {mirror_preview}.

race_context: The 7th District includes the majority of Indianapolis and Marion County and has a population of more than 757,000 {wfyi_guide}. WFYI reported it is the most racially diverse district in Indiana, with nearly one-third of residents Black and 16% Hispanic {wfyi_results}.
The Cook Political Report rates the district D+21, and Carson won in 2024 with 68% of the vote {wfyi_guide}.

In 2025, some Republicans sought to redraw the map to make the district more Republican, but state lawmakers voted the mid-cycle redistricting effort down; Carson opposed it {wfyi_guide}. Mirror Indy reported the effort failed after Indiana state senators joined Democrats in rejecting it {mirror_primary_night}.

In the May 5, 2026 Democratic primary, Carson received 62.4% of the vote, ahead of Destiny Wells (23.4%) and George Hornedo (10.5%), per NBC News results {nbc_results}. Denise Paul Hatch was also on the Democratic ballot {mirror_primary_night}.
In the May 5, 2026 Republican primary, Patrick McAuley received 84.4% of the vote to Felipe Rios's 15.6% {nbc_results}.
The Libertarian Party of Indiana nominated James Sceniak for the 7th District at its state convention in Fort Wayne in March 2026 {ipm_lp}.

Voters responding to a WFYI survey most often raised affordability, data center development and whether elected officials listen to them {wfyi_guide}. On data centers, Carson supports a moratorium in Indianapolis until developers show a positive result for the community, McAuley opposes data centers in residential areas, and Sceniak favors clearer permitting and siting rules rather than a ban {wfyi_guide}.
No debates or candidate forums for the general election were found in news coverage reviewed for this profile {wfyi_guide}.

candidates.summary: Carson, 51, is the incumbent, first elected in 2008, and is seeking a 10th term {wfyi_guide}. He lists opposing Trump administration policies, preserving Medicare and Medicaid, and bringing federal funds to Indiana as priorities {wfyi_guide}.
background: Carson is 51 and lives in Indianapolis {wfyi_guide}.
He has represented the district since 2008 {wfyi_guide}.

In a 2026 congressional letter he described himself as a former law enforcement officer {carson_ice_inquiry}. In a WFYI interview he said he is the only member of Congress who has worked in an intelligence fusion center {wfyi_guide}.

He serves on the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party {clerk_carson}, and is ranking member of the Aviation Subcommittee {carson_aviation_rm}.
path_to_ballot: Won the May 5, 2026 Democratic primary with 62.4% of the vote over Destiny Wells, George Hornedo and Denise Paul Hatch {nbc_results} {mirror_primary_night}.

items: Says he wants to preserve Medicare and Medicaid and argued that Medicaid cuts are affecting Hoosier families despite the state's budget surplus (Aug. 6, 2026 interview) {wfyi_guide}.
Said he supports a data center moratorium in Indianapolis "until they can show us that their presence in our community will yield a positive result" (Aug. 6, 2026) {wfyi_guide}.
Cosponsored the AI Data Center Moratorium Act and introduced the AI Data Center Site Selection Transparency Act of 2026 {carson_moratorium} {carson_dc_transparency}.
Urged federal regulators to reject the BlackRock/GIP acquisition of AES, saying the deal could raise utility rates {carson_aes}.
Introduced the Summer Meals for Kids Act to extend Summer EBT benefits to all states, including Indiana {carson_summer_meals}.
Said he wants federal investment in economic development and has legislation to help nonprofits offer food at lower cost {wfyi_guide}.

Said current immigration policy under the Trump administration is "riddled with xenophobia and anti-immigrant sentiment," while acknowledging national security, trafficking and cartel concerns, and called for a comprehensive system that protects asylum seekers and refugees (Aug. 6, 2026) {wfyi_guide}.
Voted against fiscal year 2026 DHS appropriations over ICE funding and sought information from DHS on ICE arrests in Indianapolis {carson_dhs_vote} {carson_ice_inquiry}.
Said he hopes to bring transportation resources to the district and supports a high-speed rail system linking Indianapolis with Louisville, Chicago or St. Louis {wfyi_guide}.
Supported the Build America 250 Act in committee, citing Bipartisan Infrastructure Law funding for IndyGo, highways and broadband {carson_build_america}.
Said he wants to protect federal contracting opportunities for small, veteran-owned, minority-owned and women-owned businesses {wfyi_guide}.
Said the president has gone beyond the 60-day War Powers window in the Iran war and that the war has raised gas and food prices (Aug. 6, 2026) {wfyi_guide}.

on_incumbent: No statements by Carson about McAuley or Sceniak were found; during the primary he responded to challengers' criticism of his donors by saying, "In fact, I have voted directly against the interests of donors" {mirror_preview}.
plans: Said that if re-elected he expects to chair the Aviation Subcommittee, depending on the election outcome {wfyi_guide}.
Said he will continue to oppose ICE practices he considers excessive and to pursue federal funds for infrastructure, education and economic development {wfyi_guide}.
endorsements_finance: Carson's committee, André Carson for Congress, raised $1,006,176 as of June 30, 2026, according to FEC data cited by WFYI, including $485,550 from PACs per OpenSecrets {wfyi_guide}.
He reported $646,000 in his campaign account at the end of 2025 {mirror_preview}.
gaps: Carson told WFYI 27 of his bills have passed and Mirror Indy that 22 bills were signed into law; neither count was independently verified for this profile.
Sources differ on his start date: WFYI says he has served since 2008, Mirror Indy says 2007.
Third-quarter 2026 FEC figures were not reviewed (FEC API rate limit).

candidates.summary: McAuley, 29, is an Indianapolis commercial real estate associate making his first run for office {wfyi_guide} {wfyi_results}. He says his priorities are housing, jobs, homelessness and public safety {wfyi_guide}.
background: McAuley is 29, lives in Indianapolis and is an associate at Broad Ripple Capital, Inc. {wfyi_guide}.
He is a North Central High School graduate and Wabash College All-American with a master's degree in international economics and finance, according to his campaign {mcauley_about}.
His campaign says he has previous experience in the U.S. Senate {mcauley_about}; Mirror Indy reported he interned for two U.S. senators {mirror_primary_night}.
path_to_ballot: Won the May 5, 2026 Republican primary with 84.4% of the vote over Felipe Rios {nbc_results}.

items: Proposes expanding housing supply, converting vacant properties to productive use, and supporting pathways off the street through partnerships and federal resources {mcauley_issues}.

Said he wants to help residents in Section 8 housing build credit to become homeowners and cited the federal Good Neighbor Next Door program and community land trusts to resell foreclosed homes to police, firefighters and teachers {wfyi_guide}.
Calls for stronger community-police relationships and more officers living in the precincts they patrol {mcauley_issues}.

Cited a 900% increase in youth gun violence since 2008; WFYI said it could not find evidence for that figure and noted consecutive years of declining shootings and homicides in Indianapolis {wfyi_guide}.
Proposes a 10-15% increase in federal resources for registered apprenticeships in the skilled trades {mirror_mcauley}.
Says expanding trades, apprenticeships and skilled-job opportunities should be a priority because not every young person needs a four-year degree {mcauley_issues}.
Said federal appropriations fund duplicate accounts, cited humanitarian aid accounts as an example, and said spending should be redirected to cities {wfyi_guide}.
Said Indiana lost more than $700 million in direct federal funding last year and that he would prioritize restoring road and infrastructure funding for urban districts {mirror_mcauley}.

Said data centers should not be placed in residential communities, citing what he has heard from constituents {wfyi_guide}. He told Mirror Indy he would support a congressional caucus focused on public communication and citizen feedback on data centers {mirror_mcauley}.
Said he is open to immigrants who come seeking opportunity and supports a standard for entry, but opposes violence by ICE agents and agents covering their faces (WFYI interview) {wfyi_guide}.
Said Indiana's elections are secure and that he supports voter ID {wfyi_guide}.

on_incumbent: Said in a WFYI interview that the district has lost 15,000 skilled-trades jobs "since my opponent's been in office"; WFYI said it found no record of that figure {wfyi_guide}.
Said that over the past 20 years of leadership in the district "no one has had oversight" of where communities are headed {wfyi_guide}.
plans: Says his platform is based on a 2025 survey of more than 400 district residents {wfyi_guide} {mcauley_about}.
Says his three main issues are public safety, housing and homelessness, and career pathways and jobs {mcauley_issues}.
endorsements_finance: WFYI found no FEC campaign committee or OpenSecrets donor data for McAuley; candidates raising or spending less than $5,000 are not required to file {wfyi_guide}.
gaps: Unverified (search snippets only): Axios Indianapolis (Oct. 8, 2026) described him as a political newcomer and a former intern for Sen. Todd Young; also listed Valparaiso University among his schools.
Unverified (search snippet only): a search summary said McAuley did not return the Indiana Capital Chronicle voter-guide survey; the page could not be loaded.
His campaign accepts donations through WinRed, but no FEC filings were confirmed; no endorsements were found.
WFYI could not confirm several figures he cited (youth gun violence, lost jobs and wages, city budget).

candidates.summary: Sceniak is a behavior therapist and vice chair of the Libertarian Party of Indiana {wfyi_guide}. His stated priorities are privacy protections, lower taxes, workforce protections and veterans' health care choice {wfyi_guide}.
background: Sceniak is a lead registered behavior therapist at Centria Health Care and vice chair of Indiana's Libertarian Party {wfyi_guide}.
WFYI lists his residence as Indianapolis {wfyi_guide}; the March 2026 convention report listed him as from Greenwood {ipm_lp}.
He described himself as a fourth-generation immigrant {wfyi_guide}.
path_to_ballot: Nominated by the Libertarian Party of Indiana at its state convention in Fort Wayne in March 2026 {ipm_lp}.

items: Said inflation and federal debt are the main affordability problems and that both parties "continually fund the spending" {wfyi_guide}.
Supports cutting spending through the "Penny Plan" associated with Sen. Rand Paul and said the Jones Act should be repealed to lower import costs {wfyi_guide}.
Said tax credits should go to individuals rather than businesses: "I don't think big corporations should get tax cuts" {wfyi_guide}.
Proposes a plan he calls "Vet Care" to give veterans more choice in their health care outside set VA procedures {wfyi_guide}.

Said data centers should pay their fair share, should not get tax cuts or be placed next to neighborhoods, and that water resources should be protected; he did not endorse a ban or moratorium, favoring clearer permitting and siting rules {wfyi_guide}.
Said there must be borders, security and a process for entry, but called current ICE tactics "absolutely unconstitutional" and said the citizenship process should be less costly {wfyi_guide}.

Said he would have voted for the House resolution to remove U.S. forces from Iran and generally opposes intervening in conflicts overseas while supporting a strong national defense (July 29, 2026 interview) {wfyi_guide}.

on_incumbent: No statements specifically about Carson were found {wfyi_guide}. Speaking generally, he said many officials who have served in Washington a long time "forget what it is to put food on the table" {wfyi_guide}.
plans: Said he would work with local officials on infrastructure and economic issues in Marion County {wfyi_guide}.
Said he takes donations only from private voters {wfyi_guide}.
endorsements_finance: WFYI found no FEC campaign committee or OpenSecrets donor data for Sceniak {wfyi_guide}.
gaps: No campaign website was found; WFYI lists facebook.com/SceniakForSenate.

Unverified (search snippets only): prior runs for U.S. Senate (2022), Greenwood City Council and Indiana's 6th District (2024) were seen only in search results and older articles not reviewed for this profile.
Residence discrepancy: Indianapolis (WFYI, Sept. 2026) vs. Greenwood (convention report, March 2026).
